summaries.example: Imagine a marble moving through a garden maze while a map helps guide its path. In Bohmian mechanics, a particle has an actual position, while its wave function helps guide how it moves. In a two-slit experiment, the particle goes through one slit, but the wave passes through both and helps create the final pattern.
summaries.summary: Bohmian mechanics is one way to understand quantum physics. It keeps the wave function used in ordinary quantum theory, but adds the actual positions of particles. A guiding equation uses the wave function to determine how those positions change. In a two-slit experiment, each particle takes one route, while the wave travels through both routes and influences where the particle lands. The theory is deterministic, but its results can look random because the starting positions are not known. It also says that ordinary measurement results can come from the motion of particles and instruments, rather than from a special rule that applies only when someone observes.
key_ideas: Bohmian mechanics says quantum theory describes real particles with actual positions, not only possibilities or observations.
The wave function guides particle motion, while the particles’ positions complete the description of a system.
The theory is deterministic: if the starting wave and positions were known, the later motion would be fixed.
Random-looking results can arise because we do not know the exact starting positions.
The usual measurement results, including wave-function collapse, can be explained without giving measurement a special mysterious role.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bohmian mechanics gives a clear picture of what quantum theory might be describing: particles moving in the ordinary world, guided by a wave. It shows that scientists can agree on many predictions while disagreeing about what is really happening underneath those predictions. Studying it helps us ask what a scientific theory should explain, not just what it should calculate.

important_terms.definition: A theory saying that particles really have positions and move along definite paths, guided by a wave function.
A mathematical description that changes over time and guides the motion of particles.
The rule that tells how a particle’s position changes as time passes.
The idea that what happens to one part of an entangled system can depend on another part, even when far away.

questions_to_think_about: If a particle follows a definite path, why might its result still look random to us?
How can a wave passing through both openings affect a particle that passes through only one?
Would you prefer a theory with invisible positions or one that talks mainly about measurements?
Why might action across a distance seem puzzling?

summaries.example: In a two-slit experiment, a single electron is detected as a localized spot, yet many electrons form an interference pattern. Bohmian mechanics says each electron has a definite position and travels through one slit. The wave function evolves through both slits according to Schrödinger’s equation; the guiding equation then directs the particle so that the distribution of arrival points matches the usual quantum prediction.
summaries.summary: Bohmian mechanics, also called the de Broglie–Bohm or pilot-wave theory, is an interpretation and formulation of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics built around two elements: a wave function obeying Schrödinger’s equation and an actual configuration of particles whose motion obeys a guiding equation. The wave function is therefore not a complete description, but it determines the velocity field in which the particles move. The theory is deterministic, while quantum statistics arise when initial configurations are distributed according to |ψ|², a distribution preserved by the dynamics. This preservation, called equivariance, allows Bohmian mechanics to recover ordinary quantum predictions. Measurement outcomes are explained by the final configurations of systems and apparatuses, so a separate measurement postulate is not fundamental. Interference follows because the wave passes through both slits even though a particle follows one path. Entanglement makes the theory explicitly nonlocal, and Bell’s work is presented as showing that locality is incompatible with the relevant quantum correlations, not that all hidden-variable theories are impossible. Important open or difficult issues include the theory’s standard lack of Lorentz invariance, its relation to quantum field theory, and how best to understand the status of the wave function.
key_ideas: The theory treats particle positions as fundamental variables and the wave function as a guiding structure. Its two basic dynamical ingredients are Schrödinger evolution and the guiding equation.

Bohmian mechanics is deterministic at the level of the wave function and particle configuration. Quantum probabilities arise from the quantum-equilibrium distribution over unknown initial configurations.
It reproduces the usual predictions of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, including interference, spin experiments, and measurement statistics, without adding measurement-specific fundamental laws.
The apparent collapse of a subsystem’s wave function can arise from its interaction with an environment and its actual configuration; this is often described as effective or conditional collapse.

Bell’s analysis does not simply rule out hidden variables. Rather, it shows that quantum theory’s correlations conflict with locality under the relevant assumptions. Bohmian mechanics makes nonlocality explicit.
The theory is not Lorentz invariant in its standard nonrelativistic form, and possible relativistic extensions involve difficult questions about nonlocality and the structure of space-time.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophical importance of Bohmian mechanics lies in the distinction between predicting outcomes and describing reality. It offers a precise ontology of particles in ordinary space and replaces fundamental measurement rules with dynamical laws, while retaining the successful quantum formalism. At the same time, it makes nonlocality unavoidable and faces challenges concerning relativity and extensions beyond nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. Comparing it with textbook and many-worlds approaches clarifies that empirical agreement does not settle every question about interpretation, explanation, or ontology.

important_terms.definition: A nonrelativistic quantum theory in which a system is described by its wave function together with the actual configuration, or positions, of its particles.
A mathematical object evolving by Schrödinger’s equation; in Bohmian mechanics it guides particle positions but is not the complete description of a system.
The dynamical law connecting the wave function to the velocities of the particles’ actual positions.
The claim that a wave function does not by itself fully describe physical reality; additional variables complete the description.
Dependence of the motion or experimental results associated with one part of an entangled system on distant parts of the system.
The quantum probability distribution proportional to the squared absolute value of the wave function, written as |ψ|².
Dependence of an experimental result on the complete experimental arrangement, rather than on a pre-existing value of an abstract observable alone.
The conceptual difficulty that ordinary quantum evolution seems to produce superpositions of different outcomes without selecting one definite result.

questions_to_think_about: Does a deterministic theory genuinely explain quantum randomness if observers lack the relevant initial conditions?
Is adding actual particle positions a clarification of quantum mechanics, a new theory, or merely a reformulation? What standards should decide?
Why does the two-slit experiment require considering both the particle’s route and the wave function’s evolution?
Does contextuality seem less mysterious if an experiment is understood as an interaction between system and apparatus?
What should count as a satisfactory solution to the measurement problem: definite outcomes, new dynamics, or a different account of the wave function?

summaries.example: Suppose a game sends a ball toward a screen with two openings. In an ordinary game, the ball chooses one opening. In a two-slit quantum experiment, the final pattern looks like waves passing through both openings. Bohmian mechanics combines these ideas: the particle has one actual route, but its guiding wave uses both openings. The wave’s pattern changes which landing places are likely.
summaries.summary: Bohmian mechanics is a version of quantum theory that tries to make the theory’s physical picture more definite. It says that particles really have positions, and that these positions change according to a guiding equation. The wave function still evolves as in ordinary quantum mechanics, but it is only part of the description. The actual particle positions complete it. This makes the theory deterministic: the wave function and initial positions determine later motion. However, people usually do not know those exact positions, so the results of experiments appear random. The theory uses the quantum-equilibrium distribution, proportional to |ψ|², to recover the usual probabilities. It also gives a way to understand the measurement problem. A measuring device is itself made of particles, and its pointer ends up in one definite configuration. What textbooks call collapse can then arise as an effective description of the subsystem. The two-slit experiment shows the theory’s central idea: a particle goes through one slit, while its wave function is affected by both. The theory’s price is nonlocality. For entangled systems, the motion associated with one part can depend on the configuration of another distant part. Bell’s work is important because it challenges local explanations of quantum correlations, not because it proves that every deterministic theory is impossible. Philosophers and physicists continue to compare Bohmian mechanics with textbook and many-worlds approaches.
key_ideas: Bohmian mechanics says that particles have definite positions even when quantum theory does not directly reveal them.
The wave function is important, but it is not the whole physical story in this theory.
The theory is deterministic, yet experiments can look random because we do not know the particles’ precise starting positions.
In a two-slit experiment, the particle takes one slit while the wave function passes through both and guides the result.
The theory explains measurement results through the motion of the system and the measuring device, rather than treating observation as a special basic event.
Bohmian mechanics accepts nonlocality, and this connects it to debates about Bell’s theorem and the limits of local explanations.
summaries.why_it_matters: This theory matters because it separates two questions that are often mixed together: what results quantum mechanics predicts and what the world is like according to the theory. Bohmian mechanics keeps the successful calculations of quantum physics while offering definite particles and a clear account of outcomes. Studying it also introduces major philosophical ideas—determinism, realism, probability, measurement, and nonlocality—and shows why scientific theories can disagree even when their tested predictions agree.

important_terms.definition: A view of quantum theory in which particles have definite positions and their motion is guided by a wave function.
A mathematical description of a quantum system that evolves over time and helps determine particle motion.
A law in Bohmian mechanics that connects the wave function with the changing positions of particles.
Extra facts added to a theory to complete a description that the wave function alone does not provide.
A feature of quantum theory in which distant parts of an entangled system can be connected in a way that cannot be explained by ordinary local influences.
The puzzle of how quantum theory gives definite experimental results if its ordinary evolution can leave several outcomes in a superposition.

questions_to_think_about: Can a theory be deterministic underneath while still giving probabilities to observers?
Why might knowing which slit a particle uses change the interference pattern?
Is a hidden variable really hidden if it represents something the theory says is physically real?
Which seems like the bigger cost: a special measurement rule or nonlocal connections?
What does it mean for two theories to make the same predictions but tell different stories about reality?
